item.title: OSCP - Algernon - Windows
item.description:
Algernon

This was my first shift across from Linux into Windows, and I’ll freely admit to being a little overwhelmed at all the open ports and not knowing quite where to start. Realising the FTP had an anonymous login was straight forward, and identifiying the admin user from the logs was nice, but it turned out to be a deadend and the real solution was 10x easier than what I’d experienced with the last few Linux boxes - I really needed to reset my expectations.

item.title: OSCP - Astronaut - Linux
item.description:
Astronaut

Much quicker and more useful experience than Exfiltrated. Did my own enumeration, and used the walkthrough only as a guide when getting stuck.

Discovering “blind” exploits was interesting, however it made sense that if the exploit isn’t generating any output and not creating a reverse shell, that you might need to add a -c command with a line of bash to establish a reverse shell instead. Although once again all the instructions were in the script if you looked - always read the script!

item.title: OSCP - Authby - Windows
item.description:
Authby

These Windows are doing my absolute head in. I spent hours on this box the day before following a multiple walkthroughs to the letter and got nowhere. I and wound up feeling so frustrated at not receiving even an initial shell that I marked this box as “Aborted” and shut down for the night - I figured there was no point pushing on and to just move on to the next Windows box.

item.title: OSCP - Blackgate - Linux
item.description:
Blackgate

This is the first of the “Hard” machines I’ve tackled, so I’d been worried it may have been a major step up from what I’d been doing previously. Surprisingly though, this was very much a case of googling and learning about a service I’d never heard of (Redis), connecting to it to test a few commands, and then finding the version I was connected to had a well known RCE exploit and using it to achieve initial access!

item.title: OSCP - Boolean - Linux
item.description:
Boolean

This was an absolute slog, and even the walkthroughs didn’t help at the end. It was good to identify that BurpSuite would be used early on, but picking up and changing the “confirmed” element was tricky. Having the PHP reverse shell not work was incredibly frustrating too, but it was obvious something else would be needed when GoBuster wasn’t showing where the uploaded files were being stored (obviously download only and not directly web accessible).

item.title: OSCP - Cheat Sheet - Core
item.description:
Pre-Exam

  • Download the resources from the dedicated lab clients;
  • Document your report as you go during the exam
  • Do a practice exam!

Setup

Create directories: mkdir dc host1 host2

  • Create sub directories: mkdir enu loot files exploits Setup hostnames: sudo nano /etc/hosts then add host/kali IPs

Quick Reference

  • sudo nmap -T5 -p- -v host1 -oN enu/host1.nmap
  • sudo nmap -T5 -p80,443,1978-1980 -sCV -v host1 -oN enu/nmap-services.nmap
  • gobuster dir -u http://host1 -w /usr/share/dirb/wordlists/common.txt | tee gobuster-p80.nmap
  • usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
  • usr/share/wordlists/SecLists
  • nc -nvlp 4444 NetCat Cheat Sheet
  • https://www.revshells.com/

Easy wins

  • Linux: Capabilities, SUIDs/GUIDs, cronjobs, modifiable binaries running as root, out-of-date binaries, known-binary exploits, history files.
  • Windows: Weak service permissions, Unquoted service paths, outdated binaries, scheduled tasks, custom
  • Take breaks, and set timers: If you’re not getting anywhere for more than half an hour, take a break. Get some fresh air, and you’ll almost definitely think of a new idea.
    • Similarly, celebrate when you make progress! If you finish a machine its a good time for a rest
  • Regularly review the information you have for a machine - key services, known version numbers, and any known credentials.
  • Document as you go - take screenshots of key moments in the machine, and of course when you read a proof file.
  • Metasploit - pick the machine that you think you have the least chance of exploiting manually

General Tips

  • xfreerdp can pass the hash to login
  • runas /user:domain\username cmd.exe (or rdp and open CMD as admin)
  • Use the Kali directory: /usr/share/webshells for all your payloads.
  • MSFVenom Shell code for Buffer Overflow https://www.offsec.com/metasploit-unleashed/alphanumeric-shellcode/
  • If it’s running SSH, find/replace the id_rsa
  • !/bin/bash
  • SMB - crackmapexec show available shares: crackmapexec smb 192.168.50.242 -u john -p "dqsTwTpZPn#nL" --shares
  • Scanning UDP Ports for SNMP - https://infosecwriteups.com/why-you-should-always-scan-udp-ports-part-1-2-d8ee7eb26727

item.title: OSCP - Clue - Linux
item.description:
Clue

This was definitely a hard box, but the biggest challenges came from the range of different services AND the box itself not working properly. After a couple of hours bashing my head against the brick wall trying to get initial access, I finally relented and looked at a walkthrough… only to find that the cassandra exploit I’d tried to use to display files on the target hadn’t worked because the box needed to be reverted.

item.title: OSCP - Cockpit - Linux
item.description:
Cockpit

This one was originally listed as “Hard” in my list, but when I checked during startup it showed as “Intermediate”. Definitely don’t think it should be listed as “Intermediate” though - this was definitely the trickest boxes I’ve done, and I absolutely leaned heavily on the walkthrough to make progress here.

The biggest challenge ofcourse was the box breaking everytime I tried to run gobuster against it to find directories or files. Turned out there was a hidden login.php file on the port 80 server, but I couldn’t find the damn thing with the first few gobuster scans because the whole box would break and require revert. Worse was finding the blocked.html page which would break the box every time I visited it OR scanned it with gobuster.

item.title: OSCP - Codo - Linux
item.description:
Codo

Interesting experience just slowly working through this over the day. Having the walkthrough as a reference is handy, although I should have done more enumeration to identify everything linpeas was providing. Helpful experience updating the cheatsheet for fully interactive TTS too - most references just use python when pretty much everyone/thing is using python3, so be sure to watch out for that when copy/pasting from references.

Keep revshells.com handy too, and keep practicing with msfvenom too, as a lot of your holdup today was trying to find the right reverse shell for php, when you should have just been able to pull it up in a heartbeat

item.title: OSCP - Crane - Linux
item.description:
Crane

This was the most straight-forward box so far. While a walkthrough was referenced for some of the exploit syntax, the exploit itself had already been found and tested before hand, so catching the reverse shell was straightforward.

After initial access, it was clear usr/sbin/service could be used for privilege escalation. It took a bit of testing, but combining www-data’s sudo privileges with directory traversal led to root access

Resolution summary

  • Scanned with Nmap to find ports 22, 80, & 3306
  • Navigated to http://192.168.137.146:80
  • Password guessed admin login, and identified SuiteCRM 7.12.3
  • Found exploit for CVE-2022-23940, executed against target & achieved shell
  • Checked sudo privileges and found /usr/sbin/services
  • Used sbin & directory traversal to escalate to root

Improved skills

  • Finding/testing exploits
  • Linux Privilege Escalation

Used tools

  • Nmap
  • NetCat

Information Gathering

Scanned all TCP ports:

item.title: OSCP - Exfiltrated - Linux
item.description:
Exfiltration

Relatively easy box turned into a VERY frustrating experience at not being able to properly execute exiftool exploit because of missing library dependencies. Exploit actually detailed exactly how to install those dependencies, but I was looking for instructions on Stack Overflow instead of in the script itself - always read the script!

Exploits were relatively straight forward once the dependencies were sorted though, so all round good practice on the process of popping boxes. Local user had also been identified by linpeas.sh but ended up getting root first (flag = proof.txt) then using root privilege to find the coaran user with GID=1000 and the local flag (flag = local.txt).

item.title: OSCP - Extplorer - Linux
item.description:
Extplorer

This was simultaneously the easiest and most frustrating box yet. Identifying and accessing filemanager was ridiculously easy, and uploading a reverse shell php and catching the shell seemed easy initially. Even finding credentials for dora was easy once I started looking through all the info that was available in the filemanager folder.

What I wasn’t expecting was to spend 2 hours trying to figure out why I couldn’t upgrade the dumb shell I’d caught to a full shell, even though I knew the target was running python3.

item.title: OSCP - Fired - Linux
item.description:
Fired

This box was relatively straightforward until the very last step, where I simply couldn’t find credentials to move forward. I needed a bit of guidance finding how to setup the admin panel to establish a reverse shell, but all the details were on an exploit page when I went looking. The walkthrough support for the box itself was very limited (or atleast I could only find a single walkthrough for it) and the only major barrier was the very final step - finding a script file in the openfire directory that had cleartext root credentials.

item.title: OSCP - Flu - Linux
item.description:
Flu

This is the first box I can confidently say I did NOT look at a walkthrough for any help on! I’ve included one in the details above, but it remained as a background tab the entire way through this - massive confidence boost to know I can do this without needing to follow someone else’s footsteps!

Seeing Confluence when I checked the html port was a big confidence booster too, as I’ve worked with it a lot already and knew there were plenty of vulnerabilities and exploit available for older versions. Getting RCE was incredibly simple, and then it was simply a case of enumerating the target to find a privilege escalation vector.

item.title: OSCP - Hub - Linux
item.description:
Hub

This was a bit of an odd one that required more than a few reverts. Identifying that FuguForum was the target (not barracuda as initially suspected) was a nice realisation that I’m picking up on the details that I need to, and that searching for exploits is becoming a more common and clear thing to do.

What was really frustrating was finding that none of those exploit actually work, and then needing to dig into the website to write a reverse shell into page. So much of this box didn’t work properly, and what should have been straight forward was unnecessarily difficult - not because it was secure, but because it simply wasn’t working properly. Even once I managed to get a shell, there was no way to upgrade it to full TTY, so once I had root through a binary exploit, I was still stuck with a shitty shell.

item.title: OSCP - Hutch - Windows
item.description:
Box

Rinse and repeat on the Windows bullshit here. Just like Authby, this was an exercise in absolute frustration yesterday - trying every possible exploit combination and following numerous walkthroughs - only for the entire thing to crack in a heartbeat tonight using the exact same tools and exploit I ran 24 hours earlier.

Once again this is a reminder that these Windows boxes are unbelievable unreliable and unstable, so if you’re following the exact steps of a walkthrough and things are not working, then shut the box down and move on. There is absolutely no point bashing your head against a broken box, so let it go.

item.title: OSCP - Image - Linux
item.description:
Image

This box was objectively quite easy, however the issues I had around it made things far more complicated/frustrating than they needed to be.

Prior to starting this box I’d tried to setup a shared folder on the VM that would also upload to Google drive (with the intent being I could pull the box folder to any desktop/laptop I was working from). However when I started running the exploit to try to create the .png with the reverse shell in the name, I started getting an error message saying the file didn’t exist.

item.title: OSCP - Internal - Windows
item.description:
Internal

These Windows boxes are getting more and more frustrating. This one I had four separate walkthroughs available and 5 different exploits I could run, and in the end I had to resort to Metasploit to catch a meterpreter shell. Even the Meterpreter shell was a pain in the ass - once I was in I knew I could navigate directly to the Administrator’s desktop, but I had to type in each directory change one-by-one rather than going directly to the proof file.

item.title: OSCP - Jacko - Windows
item.description:
Box

What the actual fuck… I’ll write this up tomorrow, but this was a combination of “Why the fuck isn’t this working” with “that is so fucking dumb” when it did finally work

Resolution summary

  • Ran Nmap to identify ports 80, 135/445, 445, 5040, 8082 & 9092
  • Navigated to port 8082 with browser and logged in with default credentials
  • Found exploit for H2 Database and achieved code execution via SQL
  • Uploaded & executed reverse shell via SQL statements for initial access
  • Identified Paperstream software and found exploit 49382.py
  • Used msfvenom to create reverse shell dll with x86 architecture & xor_dynamic
  • Uploaded dll and 49382.ps1 to target via iwr
  • Ran 49382.ps1 on target and recieved reverse shell as NT-system

Improved skills

  • Generating msfvenom payloads
  • Working with Windows kernel exploits (specifically potatos)

Used tools

  • nmap
  • python
  • msfvenom
  • powershell

Information Gathering

Scanned all TCP ports:

item.title: OSCP - Kevin - Windows (DNF)
item.description:
Kevin

I’ve checked all the walkthroughs, tried countless variations of the easily available exploits, even reimaged my entire Kali VM trying to make this script work… and nothing I’ve done has caught a reverse shell.

Honestly not sure what else to do, other than to write this off as a learning experience (?) and move on. If I get a buffer overflow exploit in the exam (which I think they’ve stopped now anyway) I’ll just move the fuck on because nothing I’ve done on this box or the last one has really made any sense.

item.title: OSCP - LaVita - Linux
item.description:
LaVita

This box started out really well with plenty of through enumeration to identify the vulnerability, but I fell down trying to gain initial access with the exploits. I tried several, and persisted with the most well developed exploit thinking it would be the way forward.

The issue was not realising the exploit would stop working after the first success, so after testing it with the uname -a or id commands, it would then not work when I tried to repeat with a reverse shell command. it took awhile to realise that there were 21 chains available, and so there was no need to keep using the “last working” chain, because it was only working once anyway. I also stopped trying to test with id and just threw the reverse shell command in straight away - I already knew the exploit worked sometimes so may as well try to establish a shell each time I tried.

item.title: OSCP - Law - Linux
item.description:
Law

This one was another absolute slog. Identifying exploits for htmLawed v1.2.5 was very straightforward, and I got a little excited when I saw an RCE exploit had been found this year (2024).

Running the exploit didn’t work though, so I started researching the vulnerability further while trying to avoid the walkthroughs. I found the Mayfly article on the CVE which added a lot of extra context, and checking the walkthrough helped me realise why the Burpsuite request wasn’t working properly (the request was to a non-existent page, and needed to be changed to /).

item.title: OSCP - Levram - Linux
item.description:
Levram

Resolution summary

  • Nmap to identify services on port 22 and 8000
  • Password guessed admin credentials to Gerapy platform
  • Used exploit for CVE-2021-243857 to achieve shell
  • Upgraded shell by running bash script on target
  • Identified vulnerable python setuid configuration
  • Used GTFObins to find python command providing privilege escalation to root

Improved skills

  • Linux Privilege Escalation
  • Establishing Full TTYs

Used tools

  • nmap
  • python
  • linpeas.sh
  • gerapy
  • GTFObins

Information Gathering

Scanned all TCP ports:

item.title: OSCP - Ochima - Linux
item.description:
Ochima

This one was an exercise in frustration purely because the exploit didn’t seem to work on the port I wanted it to (4444) but would work on port 80!?

I tired all sorts of things to get it work, the walkthroughs didn’t explain why they used port 80, and the exploit itself indicated it’d work on whatever I picked… but the moment I popped port 80 into the exploit’s reverse shell parameters I got an incoming connection. So an important reminder that if a reverse shell isn’t working on port 4444 then try the same thing but with a listener on port 80 instead

item.title: OSCP - PC - Linux
item.description:
PC

This was an interesting one, with linpeas showing multiple vulnerabilities and yet the most obvious two didn’t work because of missing dependencies and no user credentials.

Figuring out how rpcpy-exploit worked was interesting, but the real lesson here was understanding how if the SUID binary can be set then you can run Bash in privileged mode with /bin/bash -p and become root

Resolution summary

  • Ran Nmap to identify ports 22 & 8000
  • Visited http (8000) & identified ttyd
  • Created reverse shell and enumerated target
  • Ran linpeas.sh and identified multiple vulnerabilities and rpc.sh script
  • Identified exploit for rpc.sh and used it to modify /bin/bash set permission
  • Used /bin/bash -p to switch to root

Improved skills

  • Identifying vulnerabilities & scripts with linpeas.sh

Used tools

  • nmap
  • ttyd
  • python

Information Gathering

Scanned all TCP ports:

item.title: OSCP - Pelican - Linux
item.description:
Pelican

Pretty happy with this one considering I figured most of it out without really looking at a walkthrough. Identifying Exhibition vs Zookeeper was a little confusing, but as soon as I identified that Exhibition v1.0 was vulenerable to command injection then finding & using an exploit (which was really just adding a reverse shell to a java script field) became fairly straightforward.

Privilege escalation with gcore was a little tricky, as it’s been awhile since I needed to remember how strings worked. But once it became clear I could search for plaintext passwords then it made sense and switching to root was easy.

item.title: OSCP - Plum - Linux
item.description:
Plum

This one was relatively easy to achieve initial access on, but enumerating the target once I had initial access was frustrating. I’d learned on the previous box that I could pull up locally stored mail by visiting /var/mail but hadn’t quite realised that it should be part of my standard privesc process.

Anyway, once I got the nudge from the walkthrough to check mail, it became straight-forward to switch to root and grab the flag, but 100% an important lesson in seeing the var/mail/www-data in the Linpeas output and being sure to read the mail incase there’s anything important or useful (like credentials) saved there.

item.title: OSCP - PyLoader - Linux
item.description:
PyLoader

I’m still shocked at how quick and incredibly easy this was - I went from boot to root in <15mins!

After Nmap showed responses to 22 and 9666 I checked 9666 in Firefox immediately (while the Nmap scan is still running) as I’m prone to doing for anything I don’t immediately recognise. As soon as I saw a page with pyLoad I just threw “pyload exploit” into Google, found a bunch of RCE exploits for CVE-2023-0297, and pulled up the entry on Exploit-DB.

item.title: OSCP - RubyDome - Linux
item.description:
RubyDome

Frustrating that a couple of key points in this box were only broken through with the use of the walkthrough. Throwing 127.0.0.1 into the website to break it was a new one (something to keep in mind for the future) but I’d have never worked out without the walkthrough.

Likewise the exploit initially appeared to be working perfectly but wasn’t catching a shell, and it turned out I had to add “pdf” onto the end of the target web address.

item.title: OSCP - Scrutiny - Linux
item.description:
Scrutiny

This whole box felt like a whole lot of enumeration - digging through files to find SSH keys and cleartext passwords. Probably the biggest lesson I learned out of it however was how to setup and run python libraries in a virtual environment!

The exploit required urllib3 faker to run, and python3 kept throwing the externally managed error that drove me crazy awhile back when I was trying to install the bzz library - I must have found another way around that, but this time around I actually dug into what this error was all about. Turns out python likes to run it’s external libraries in a self-contained virtual environment, and while there is an override pretty much everyone on stackoverflow was screaming that it’d break the system.

item.title: OSCP - Squid - Windows
item.description:
Squid

Everything about this box was a refresher, and there’s no doubt I leaned heavily on the walkthrough as I was doing it. Learning about Squid and spose.py was interesting, but there’s a concern that spose.py is pretty niche and I may never have found it (or realised I needed it) without the walkthrough.

Maybe it’s just more familiarity though, and with more practice I’ll get better at knowing how to tackle different Windows services. There’s no question I learned more about how proxies work from this box, and setting up FoxyProxy to reach the target’s open ports was particularly interesting.

item.title: OSCP - Twiggy - Linux
item.description:
Twiggy

Went down the rabbit hole with port 80 & port 8000 too quickly, thinking this would require SQL injection or some sort of weird user enumeration to get into a web platform.

Turns out the I needed to run nmap again with a full port scan (-p- -T5) and pick up ALL the ports before an aggressive service scan (-A -p 22,55,ect).

2nd scan picked up 4505 and 4506 which correspond to ZeroMQ ZMTP 2.0 (saltStack). Looking up Saltstack showed a vulnerability (CVE-2020-11652)

item.title: Palau
item.description:
About

Best time to go is May (Rubens) Palau offers year-round diving, but the dry season from October to May is considered the best time to visit. During this period, divers can expect calmer seas, better visibility (often exceeding 30 meters), and a higher likelihood of encountering diverse marine life.

Palau’s Rock Islands, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, are characterized by uplifted coral limestone formations that have been sculpted over millions of years by natural processes such as erosion, tidal action, and sea-level changes. This has resulted in a stunning karst topography featuring mushroom-shaped islands, caves, sinkholes, and underground channels. These formations are not only geologically significant but also contribute to the rich biodiversity and unique ecosystems found in the region

item.title: Patreon - Speaking for Free
item.description:
from email 2018-02-27

Over the last two years I’ve had a couple of fairly nasty experiences with friends and colleagues asking me to speak at their STEM event.

My general rule for the last few year has been to charge everyone booking me to speak, even if it’s just a small amount, because as soon as money is involved everyone (schools in particular) take things much more seriously. When they’re paying for your time, people make sure the presentation room is ready for you, the projector is working, and the kids are prepped. Teachers get their shit together when something is coming out of their budget, and because they’re so focused on doing their jobs they also tend to dismiss anything they’re getting for free. Zero dollars, zero investment.

item.title: Photogrammetry
item.description:
Ideas

  • Photogrammetry - Rig Setup For a dedicated Windows photogrammetry box:
  • Install NVIDIA Studio Drivers (not Game Ready)
  • Disable Windows sleep/hibernation
  • Set Power Plan to High Performance
  • Exclude project folders from Windows Defender scanning
  • Disable automatic reboots for updates
  • Put your project cache/scratch on a separate NVMe drive

Other

  • Share models on Soggy Wombats Website

Software

  • Metashape
    • Buy Metashape Pro? & run Metashape Cloud?
  • Reality Capture
    • Free it but can’t do spherical/360 images
  • Postshot

Data Storage & Processing

  • On-Prem: SSD storage in a NAS (see Gear)
    • Citrix to remotely access home server?

About

  • Algarve coastal sea caves:
    Best between June and September, when visibility is highest and seas are calm. This is when marine traffic is highest too, so early or late in this period is best for quieter exploration.
  • Inland karst systems (e.g., Mira de Aire, Serras de Aire e Candeeiros):
    Access is best in spring and autumn (April–June, September–October) when groundwater levels are manageable and temperatures mild. Winter rains can flood systems, and summer can see restrictions due to fire risk or access limits.
  • Water Temperatures: Range from 14–26°C depending on depth and region, so a 5–7mm wetsuit or drysuit is advised for inland cave systems, even in summer.
  • Local Festivals & Holidays: Avoid major holiday periods (especially August) to reduce crowds and booking difficulties.

Why: Volcanic island with isolated limestone bands and possible lava tubes intersecting freshwater lenses.

  • Status: Known dry caves and lava tubes, but freshwater cave diving is almost nonexistent.
  • Potential: Search for anchialine pools or submerged karst pockets inland or near coastal freshwater springs.
  • Best Season: May to October (dry season).

Caves

  • Source de la Rivière Sainte-Suzanne, -20.9065, 55.6017, Strong resurgence on eastern slopes; spring-fed river emerging from volcanic fissure.
  • Source Bras Cabot (Salazie Cirque), -21.0003, 55.5376, High-altitude spring at base of basalt cliffs; potentially linked to perched aquifer system.
  • Source de la Rivière des Roches, -21.0084, 55.6661, Powerful spring from fractured basalt; popular canyoning area with high discharge.
  • Source du Bras de Cilaos, -21.1422, 55.4749, Resurgence below vertical cliffs in Cilaos cirque; likely fracture-controlled groundwater flow.
  • Takamaka Valley Spring, -21.0431, 55.6356, Remote and high-flow spring at base of volcanic wall; difficult access, high potential for unexplored source conduit.
  • Source de Grand Galet (Langevin Falls), -21.2856, 55.7083, Large spring-fed cascade; major discharge from volcanic plateau into Langevin River.
  • Source de Bras d’Annette, -21.0624, 55.6078, Spring in upper Takamaka basin; steep terrain with high groundwater flow potential.
  • Source de Bras Patience, -21.1187, 55.6081, Perennial spring from cliffside in upper Ravine Blanche; minor but consistent discharge.
  • Source Ravine Citron Galet, -21.1396, 55.6362, Emergent spring in deep ravine near Grand Étang; high rainfall recharge zone.
  • Source de la Plaine des Palmistes, -21.1123, 55.6379, Widespread seepage and spring outflows on elevated plateau; volcanic aquifer discharge zone.

item.title: Rwanda
item.description:
HIGH RISK - ALL KNOWN KARST <10KM FROM Democratic Republic of Congo

About

Karst around Bugarama and Nyungwe Forest

  • Why: Karst features in the southwest near the Congo border, with known limestone outcrops.
  • Status: Almost no documented speleology or diving.
  • Potential: Blue holes and flooded sinkholes possibly linked to geothermal springs.
  • Best Season: June to September (Long Dry season)

Why June to September?

  • Dry Conditions:
    Rwanda has two dry seasons — the long dry season (June to September) and a shorter one (December to February). The long dry season offers the most stable weather, lowest rainfall, and easiest overland travel, which is essential when accessing remote or undeveloped cave sites.
  • Reduced Flood Risk:
    In karst systems, dry seasons reduce the chance of sudden flooding, improve visibility, and lower flow rates in submerged passages — critical factors for safe cave diving.
  • Cool but Comfortable Climate:
    Rwanda’s elevation means temperatures are generally mild year-round (20–27°C in the day), but the dry season offers the most reliable surface conditions for expedition logistics.

Important Cave Diving Context for Rwanda

  • Emerging or Untapped Potential:
    Rwanda is not currently a mainstream cave diving destination, but it does have significant volcanic and karst features — especially around the Northwest (Musanze) and Western regions (near Lake Kivu and Nyungwe Forest). Several lava tube caves like Musanze Caves exist, and while most are explored on foot, they may include submerged sections not yet fully mapped.
  • Exploratory Diving:
    Any cave diving in Rwanda is likely to be exploratory in nature, potentially requiring permits, environmental approvals, and collaboration with local authorities or researchers.
  • Access & Logistics:
    Remote locations, lack of existing dive infrastructure, and the potential need for self-supported expeditions (including rebreathers or portable compressors) make timing your trip for the dry season even more important.

Other Considerations

  • Permits & Conservation:
    Rwanda is extremely conservation-focused — engaging with the Rwanda Development Board (RDB) or local geologists would be essential for any diving expedition.
  • Rainy Season (March–May, October–November):
    Avoid these months. Roads may become impassable, visibility drops, and cave flooding becomes a serious risk.

1. Musanze Region (Northern Province)

  • Geological Features: This area is characterized by extensive lava tubes formed from ancient volcanic activity, particularly from the Bisoke and Sabyinyo volcanoes.
  • Notable Caves:
    • Musanze Caves: Approximately 2 km long with 31 known entrances, these caves are part of the lava basaltic layers and are the most frequently visited in Rwanda.
    • Ubuvumo Bwibihonga: The longest cave in Rwanda, featuring a multi-level system of parallel lava tubes.
  • Exploration Potential: While these caves are primarily known for dry exploration, the presence of lava tubes suggests potential for submerged sections, especially during the rainy season when water levels rise. (Visit Rwanda)

2. Nyungwe Forest Region (Western Rwanda)

  • Geological Features: This region is part of the Albertine Rift and is characterized by ancient Precambrian rocks, including quartzite and schist. While traditional karst formations are less common here, the area’s complex geology may host unique subterranean features.
  • Exploration Potential: Limited information is available about caves in this region, suggesting an opportunity for pioneering exploration.

The northwestern and western parts of Rwanda, particularly near the Volcanoes National Park and along the Albertine Rift, contain limestone and dolomitic formations associated with the uplifted sedimentary sequences of the rift system.

item.title: Script - Cave Finder - Muna Island
item.description:
import json
import requests
import csv
import time

API_KEY = 'YOUR GOOGLE API'  # Replace with your API key

# Keywords likely to return cave/sinkhole/bathing spring results
KEYWORDS = [
    'goa', 'gua', 'lubang', 'sumur alam', 'serambi alam',
    'lembah', 'grotto', 'cave', 'hole',
    'loji', 'koo', 'luban', 'permandian'
]

# Approximate coverage of Muna Island
TILE_LOCATIONS = [
    '-4.783,122.566',  # Raha
    '-5.000,122.500',  # Southwest
    '-4.600,122.700',  # Northeast
    '-4.900,122.700'   # Southeast
]

RADIUS = 50000  # 50km radius — max allowed
OUTPUT_CSV = 'muna_island_places.csv'

def search_places(keyword, location, radius, token=None):
    url = 'https://maps.googleapis.com/maps/api/place/nearbysearch/json'
    params = {
        'key': API_KEY,
        'keyword': keyword,
        'location': location,
        'radius': radius,
    }
    if token:
        params['pagetoken'] = token
  
    response = requests.get(url, params=params)
    return response.json()
  
def collect_all_places():
    all_results = [] 
    for location in TILE_LOCATIONS:
        for keyword in KEYWORDS:
            print(f"Searching for '{keyword}' near {location}")
            data = search_places(keyword, location, RADIUS)
            all_results.extend(data.get('results', []))
  
            while 'next_page_token' in data:
                time.sleep(2)
                token = data['next_page_token']
                data = search_places(keyword, location, RADIUS, token)
                all_results.extend(data.get('results', []))
  
    # Deduplicate by place_id
    deduped = {place['place_id']: place for place in all_results}
    return list(deduped.values())
  
def save_to_csv(places, filename):
    fieldnames = ['name', 'address', 'latitude', 'longitude', 'types', 'place_id']
    with open(filename, 'w', newline='', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fieldnames)
        writer.writeheader()
        for place in places:
            writer.writerow({
                'name': place.get('name'),
                'address': place.get('vicinity'),
                'latitude': place['geometry']['location']['lat'],
                'longitude': place['geometry']['location']['lng'],
                'types': ', '.join(place.get('types', [])),
                'place_id': place.get('place_id')
            })
  
if __name__ == '__main__':
    results = collect_all_places()
    save_to_csv(results, OUTPUT_CSV)
    print(f"\nSaved {len(results)} unique places to '{OUTPUT_CSV}'")

    print(f"\nSaved {len(places)} unique cave-related places to '{OUTPUT_FILE}'")

item.title: Script - Python - search-replace
item.description:
#!/usr/bin/env python3

from pathlib import Path

import argparse

import re

  

def slugify(text: str) -> str:

    """Replace spaces with dashes and strip leading/trailing spaces."""

    return text.strip().replace(" ", "-")

  

def process_file(path: Path, pattern: re.Pattern, repl_func, dry_run: bool) -> int:

    """

    Returns number of replacements made in this file.

    """

    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")

    updated, n = pattern.subn(repl_func, text)

    if n > 0 and not dry_run:

        path.write_text(updated, encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")

    return n

  

def main():

    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(

        description="Replace [[text]] with #text (spaces become dashes) in markdown files."

    )

    ap.add_argument("text", help="Search term inside [[...]] to replace (e.g., 'Bucket List').")

    ap.add_argument("--root", default=".", help="Root folder to scan (default: current directory).")

    ap.add_argument("--recursive", action="store_true", help="Recurse into subfolders.")

    ap.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true", help="Show what would change, but don't write files.")

    ap.add_argument("--ignore-case", action="store_true", help="Match [[text]] case-insensitively.")

    args = ap.parse_args()

  

    root = Path(args.root).resolve()

    pattern_glob = "**/*.md" if args.recursive else "*.md"

  

    # Build regex that matches [[<text>]], allowing for internal spaces

    flags = re.IGNORECASE if args.ignore_case else 0

    escaped = re.escape(args.text)

    needle = r"\[\[\s*" + escaped.replace(r"\ ", r"\s+") + r"\s*\]\]"

    pattern = re.compile(needle, flags=flags)

  

    # Replacement function (keeps proper slug formatting)

    def repl_func(match):

        return "#" + slugify(args.text)

  

    files = sorted(root.glob(pattern_glob))

    total_files = 0

    changed_files = 0

    total_replacements = 0

  

    for f in files:

        if not f.is_file():

            continue

        total_files += 1

        n = process_file(f, pattern=pattern, repl_func=repl_func, dry_run=args.dry_run)

        total_replacements += n

        if n > 0:

            changed_files += 1

            print(f"[UPDATED{'' if not args.dry_run else ' (dry)'}] {f.name} (+{n})")

        else:

            print(f"[SKIPPED] {f.name}")

  

    print(f"\nDone. Files scanned: {total_files}. Files changed: {changed_files}. Replacements: {total_replacements}.")

    if args.dry_run:

        print("No files were written (dry run). Use without --dry-run to apply changes.")

  

if __name__ == "__main__":

    main()

item.description:
Methologies

PASTA - Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis Focuses on aligning considerations of business objectives with technical requirements.

STRIDE - Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, DoS, Elevation Focuses on identifying what can fail in the system being modelled.

OWASP - Open Web Application Security Project Focuses on identifying possible threats, prioritizing risks, and planning mitigation strategies. It is mainly used with web and desktop applications.

  • Determine assessment scope
  • Identify threat agents.
  • Identify potential attacks.
  • Identify exploitable vulnerabilities.
  • Prioritize identified risks.
  • Mitigate risks.

item.title: Tommy Graham's Cave - 6N56
item.description:
To Do

Diving Dry Photogrammetry

About

Description: May have more sumps (See DiverNet article)

Where it is & what it is
On the WA Nullarbor near Cocklebiddy; entrance on the lip of a doline with a long haul down to water. Expect a dry entrance slope through breakdown to a lake, then multiple sumps and at least one intervening airspace.

  • Steep entrance → main chamber → lake → ~190 m sump through a phreatic maze → large dry chamber (~80 m) with another lake at far end. Beyond, Glacier Lake reportedly sumps ~130 m to a ~30 m dia. rock-pile chamber that’s blocked ~35 m above water (suggests a collapsed dome with potential bypasses).

item.title: Tonga
item.description:
About

Best time is April to October (Dry season). Excellent visibility and the chance to encounter humpback whales during their migration (June to November).

Tonga’s geological landscape includes islands with uplifted coral limestone formations, leading to the development of karst topography characterized by caves, sinkholes, and underground drainage systems. Notably, ʻEua Island exhibits extensive limestone formations with karst features, including numerous caves formed through the dissolution of carbonate rocks.

Caves

Cathedral Cave (ʻEua Island)

item.title: Tunisia
item.description:
About

🪨 Limestone Karst and Caves in Tunisia

Tunisia’s karst topography is primarily found in its central and western regions, characterized by extensive limestone and dolomite formations. These areas host numerous caves formed through karstification processes.(geologyscience.com)

  • Djebel Serj: Located in central Tunisia, this limestone mountain is home to significant cave systems, including the Ain Dhab and Mine caves. The Mine Cave is considered the longest in Tunisia, extending over 4 kilometers. (en.wikipedia.org, en.wikipedia.org)
  • Jebel Bargou: Adjacent to Djebel Serj, this area also features karstic formations with caves developed in Aptian limestone. (en.wikipedia.org)
  • Cave Nefza: Situated in the northwest, this cave extends approximately 310 meters and showcases various speleothems. (en.wikipedia.org)

These karst systems are significant both geologically and hydrologically, contributing to the region’s groundwater resources. (link.springer.com)

SQL Injection (SQLi) [A03:2021-Injection]

SQL vulnerabilities allow attackers to insert malicious SQL commands to exfiltrate, modify, or delete data. Some hackers use SQL to gain root access to the target system. The most common vulnerability is using unsanitized user inputs. Strip out any element in user-supplied inputs that the server could execute as SQL code by using Prepared Statements.

item.title: Website - Mars One preparation List
item.description: Recently I’ve had a lot of folks asking if I’m “doing any training to prepare” ahead of Mars One’s next selection phase, and I tell them that every single thing I’ve done since I heard about Mars One in early September 2012 has been about preparing for life on Mars. What they really mean though is “Are you trying to get as physically fit as possible?”. The truth is I’m not even remotely as fit as I was in my mid-20’s training with the Royal Marine Commandos, and right now I don’t want to be.

item.title: Website - Martian Stunt
item.description:
By Josh, on February 4th, 2016

About 4 months ago I got a phone call from the folks at 20th Century Fox: “Can we lock you in a small, purpose-built Mars habitat in the middle of a city and have you pretend to be Mark Watney for 5 days?”

I said yes.

Now that the mini-site www.bringhimhome.com.au is live, I can finally share with you all what I’ve been working on all this time but had to keep quiet. To mark the release of “The Martian” on Blu-ray, DVD and Digital HD; from this Monday I’ll be living inside a mock Mars habitat built on Sydney’s circular quay for 5 days, surviving in isolation through a variety of science & engineering challenges.

item.title: Website – 101 Things (79 Speed Dating) The Mighty Ginge
item.description: College Of Awesome – 101 Things (#79 Speed Dating) As much as it pains me to admit it – it’s Valentine’s Day tomorrow. And while last week’s Ron Burgundy Day tried to get the sex back into sexual harassment, there’s still plenty of people out there turning to Valentine’s Day for some old-fashioned commercialised romance. So instead of raging any further about the dubious history of St. Valentine’s Day, I’d like to suggest an alternative for those of you that failed to get laid from yelling “I WANT TO BE ON YOU” last week – speed dating. Now speed dating has a fair nasty stigma – dozens of guys and girls having “mini-dates” of 3-5 minutes, then ticking a secret ballot paper to say who they’d like to share contact details with – could be seen as slightly sleazy. But as someone who went speed dating at university (and had a damn good time doing it), I discovered it’s all in how you approach it. Most people went trying to meet the love of their life – I went to mess with other single people, and met a girl I lived with for 2 years. So if you are considering going speed dating to help numb the loneliness tomorrow, I have a few suggestions to turn what could be an uncomfortable and ultimately disappointing experience (and that’s just the cry-wank you have when you get home), into a few hours of random/memorable hilarity. Hell, you might even get laid out of it… Go For A Laugh, Not A Lay Sure, it’s got “dating” on the end of it – but who said speed dating has to be about romance? I went because A) The girl organising it is an old friend, B) She’d had someone drop out last-minute and need even numbers of guys to girls, and C) I thought it would be hilarious trying to convince every girl I met that I was born in the Andes and raised by mountain goats till I was 5. I had no intention of trying to meet someone – I’d just started my last year of university, was president of the most infamous social club on campus, and my project supervisor had just  vaporised without warning over the summer to another university. This was purely to help out a friend and have a laugh at the expense of others – the signs of a true gentleman. Go speed dating to meet crazy people, or just people in general. Go and see if you can convince someone you have a psychic link to spider monkeys (or lemurs in my case). Take a friend and dare each other to tell more and more elaborate lies. Just don’t go planning to meet the Captain of the SS Loveboat during a date shorter than most songs. Unless of course you’re telling people you are the Captain of the SS Loveboat, in which case please continue. I’m sure it’ll help you to… Be Memorable You’re about to meet more than a dozen members of the opposite sex, and you have 3-5 minutes to make a decision if you’d want them to call you. This is some high-pressure decision-making – fuck up and you could wind up inviting the girl who eats her toenails around for dinner with your parents, or sleeping with the guy who collects your hair for his extensive home-made doll collection. So you want to make a fast and memorable impression. But because you’re not trying to get them to home with you, you don’t need to stress about making a good impression. Of the 20 girls there, I remember just 4 of them; - The crazy blonde chick, who grabbed my ballot paper the moment I sat down and drew a cartoon elephant yelling “WEE-OR!” - The hockey-worshipping Canadian - The American who’d grown up in Indonesia and come to support the Canadian - The cranky brunette who I met last, spilt my drink on, and about 3 seconds before the night ended discovered had a shared interest in hiking. I have no idea if these were the most attractive/sweetest/most appropriate potential partners out of all the women there – all I know is they were the most interesting and memorable. The Canadian and American had it relatively easy because obviously being foreign alone made them more distinctive/memorable. And the cranky brunette was memorable simply because she was such a sour bitch. Sure, it was the end of the night and everyone had kind of had enough. And yes, I’d drunk enough to tranquillise a bull elephant by that stage. But scowling at someone on a 3 minute date? If I wanted to get judgemental glares from attractive women while I was drunk, I’d have started turning up to my psychology tutorials again. No, the really interesting one here is the blonde that drew the elephant. Now it’s not deliberate discrimination, but I have to admit I’ve never really been attracted to blonde women – my mum is blonde, and most of my friends in school were blonde girls and have always stayed friends. I’ve met a few “hot blondes” since leaving high school, but it was really the brunettes and redheads that kick-started this puberty party. So cartoon-elephant-drawing blonde girl was already heading into the friend zone before I’d sat down – that non-existent friend-zone I was using because I was just there for my own twisted amusement. But I distinctly remember her: even though she was one of the girls I met early in the night six years ago, and I’ve never had any contact with her again; I remember her because grabbing someone’s ballot paper and drawing a yelling cartoon elephant on it is a completely mental thing to do. I want to point out of course the elephant was the one yelling “WEE-OR!”, not her. But in retrospect I probably would have shared my details with her if she  had yelled “WEE-OR!” during our 3 minute date, because god knows that one would have been a keeper. Get Your Drunk On Alcohol – the cause and solution to all of the world’s problems. Sure, cranky-hiking-brunette didn’t appreciate me cheekily slurring and spilling my precious Southern Comfort everywhere – but if I hadn’t been drunk when I met her, I probably would have told her how absurdly dull she was. And I sure as shit wouldn’t have remembered her. So in this case alcohol stopped me from being rude to someone and helped me remember who they were. I’d highly recommend having a few drinks through the night, but maybe pace yourself. Remember you’re looking at 2-3 hours of social lubrication here. So when you have a break “to go to the bar” at the hour mark, maybe order a soft drink instead of the round of tequila shots I did. Maybe don’t start drinking 3 hours before “for courage”. And maybe don’t start stealing the drinks of your dates to “check for poison” because you’re not being a modern-day gentleman, your paving the way to rehab. Other than that, go out and have fun! Speed dating is a real blast – you’ll meet some fascinating people and have lots of laughs. And make sure you have lots of laughs. Because there’s no way you’ll be laughing when you wake up on the morning of the 15th, missing patches of hair and surrounded by your new boyfriend’s hand-made dolls. - Share this: - digg - Neal Ahh, that brought back some university memories, especially those Psychology tutorials. - The Mighty Ginge And to think they let me keep studying it for a further two years… - Menstrual Mondays – Ginger Tide | The Mighty Ginge […] over the weeks like a conveyor-belt of sexually frustrated rage. And two weeks back I published a “College Of Awesome” post about speed dating - specifically scheduled for the day before Valentines Day. item.title: Website – How to Ruin Christmas
item.description: This is the final post of the year. The Mighty Ginge will be on break until January 17th,2011 –looking forward to seeing you all next year with new site features and new posts. Merry Christmas,and try to avoid killing yourselves over the New Year. The Mighty Ginge Task Ruin the annual yule-tide festivities through a series of increasingly disrespectful and socially-misguided acts. Background Christmas –a time to share with friends,family and reindeer. It’s the season for togetherness,appreciating those close to you,for generosity and empathy. It’s also the time of the year when people go batshit insane. Shopping,dinners,cards,letters –people are travelling and sending shit everywhere. They get together with family because “they have to”,put up with Grandad’s violent,racist and mysoginistic outbursts for the sake of “harmony”,send out bulk emails to people they don’t even talk to,break the bank buying gifts for kids who play with the box instead,and then take them to sit on the knee of some red-suited paedophile who talks about the goodies in his sack that he’ll give them if they’re good. So in response to this insanity,I’ve compiled a variety of ways you can strike back at the spirit of Saint Nic. These are merely suggestions and guidelines based on previous experiences however –I strongly encourage you all to create or recount your own misadventures,and post them in the comments below. Hitting the Fat Man where it hurts Disclaimer:As this is an entry level experience,I recommend starting out here for those looking to ruin their first Christmas. If at the end you feel any emotion other than malicious joy,I would recommend avoiding any of the other techniques and simply continuing to be passive aggressive at Christmas dinner when passing the salt. “Hitting the Fat Man”requires a high visibility and very large inflatable Santa Claus. Ideally the giant Santa will be located somewhere with limited physical access,but with massive visual impact –for example on the top of a shopping centre facing a freeway. You will need; - A lightweight ladder (or mad ninja skills) - A large,plain white sheet - Black spraypaint - Two bricks - Several meters of string. On Christmas eve,approach your target Santa from low ground below the sight line of any security cameras/roving patrols,and get access to the roof. This can either be by lifting yourself on the edge of a doorframe in a loading bay,hanging off the external grate of a nearby airvent and then swinging your legs onto the roof to pull yourself up backwards (eg. Generally being Sam Fisher);or bringing a ladder with you. Ensure though that you can pull the ladder onto the roof with you if you do use it though,least it be spotted by a roaming security guard. Once on the roof,tie the string to the corners of the sheet and use the bricks to hold the string in place,spreading the sheet out along the wall facing the freeway under Santa’s feet. Now spraypaint “SANTA ISN’T REAL –MERRY XMAS”in foot tall letters on the white sheet,climb back down the ladder/airvent,and make your escape. Chances are it will stay up there for 3 days,because the shopping centre needs to hire an elevated work platform to legally access that part of the roof. The Facade Breaker Extended family:you can’t pick them,but you can ensure they never speak to you again. Christmas with big families is usually a fairly stressful event for everyone,so save yourself the trouble of false pre tense and feigned respect –tell them what you think of them. For example if you’re 8 and having Christmas at your Grandad’s,playing with a water hose and enjoying a hot Australian summer,and he suddenly comes out of the kitchen with a carving knife in his hand screaming that you’ll kink the hose –tell your parents you’re scared of him (like the rest of the family),and that you won’t come out of a spider-infested caravan until he dies or they take you home. Alternatively,inform your parents every year that you’d rather be raped by a thousand angry Squirrel monkeys that see extended family for Christmas. When they finally do convince you that 5 days in a holiday home with them is survivable,give it a real chance. Stay quiet when the pointed questions about your career start;play the game when plans get changed at the last minute to suit the selfish needs of a few;bite your tongue when your the relatives start getting overly religious –it’s okay,your time will come. Because on Christmas night –when everyone is gathered around having a roast and your god-bothering Aunty steps up her week long campaign of bitchiness by accusing your Mum of trying to steal her children away –you get to step up and tell her to “stop acting like such a fucking child”,and that “everyone is sick of your shit”. When she demands you respect her because she’s your aunty,inform her that you respect people who deserve it (eg. not middle aged women who act like children),then storm out of the house. If your not sure that will get you cut off from family Christmases,make sure you rub salt in the wound by apologising to your aunt the next morning for the language you used,but make a point that you still think she’s acts like child and that you don’t care if she thinks it’s disrespectful,she can still fuck off. Seriously,let that shit out –a little work early on will save you a lifetime of awkward Christmas conversations and annual attempts to justify yourself to people you don’t like just because you share genetic material. Spread the Malice Just because you’ve been banned from any future family yule-tide gatherings doesn’t mean you can’t spread your own unique brand of Christmas cheer to other families. Ofcourse not being part of the family makes it more difficult to expose their insecurities:why not expose your own? A favourite of mine is to run away from your long term girlfriend to another state “just for Summer”when she needs you most,and break up with her two week before Christmas from the other side of the country. Then it’s important to get absurdly drunk at the Christmas dinner of the family friends you’re staying with,spill hard liquor on their grandmother,and sing out of tune Disney classics on Singstar with their nieces. To top it off,make sure you then sleep with one of the nieces on Boxing Day and get a photo of her sitting on your lap posted on facebook for your still-grieving ex to see. Not only will your parents be personally horrified,but you’ll have spoiled Christmas for two other families too. The company of strangers Congratulations of getting this far –you’ve worked hard. Now that you can’t go home for Christmas and friends won’t invite you around because you’re a liability,the final stage is to ruin Christmas with people you’ve just met! Book a room in a youth hostel,get drunk and fuck some hideous French girl who doesn’t know enough English to say no! Go back the next year and remind the hostel staff that none of them have moved on their lives! Start fights with the homeless! If you’re in a foreign country,abuse the good intentions of others by tagging along with a friend who you haven’t seen since school,then wage a week long war against their cat. The world is your oyster –people will welcome you into their homes out of charity,and shoo you back out less certain of man’s inherent good nature. Just don’t do anything I wouldn’t do. MERRY CHRISTMAS FROM THE MIGHTY GINGE - Share this: - StumbleUpon - Digg - Reddit - Jessica Actually,I thought the first step was the hardest. I like kids and some of them are still innocent,so I wouldn’t want to ruin THEIR Christmas. But,yeah,I have no problem ruining the Christmas of adults that should know better. Although I’m sure I’ll continue to be passive agressive…
